questiontext.text:
For each pair of events, decide whether they are mutually exclusive, independent, or neither.

Event B: [[if test="is(i1=1)"]]it shows 5[[elif test="is(i1=2)"]]she goes on foot[[elif test="is(i1=3)"]]the number is a multiple of 10[[elif test="is(i1=4)"]]the learner is in Grade 12[[elif test="is(i1=5)"]]the die shows 6[[elif test="is(i1=6)"]]the second toss is heads[[elif test="is(i1=7)"]]Amina's spinner lands on red[[elif test="is(i1=8)"]]the second seed germinates[[elif test="is(i1=9)"]]the score is less than 4[[elif test="is(i1=10)"]]the road to school is muddy[[elif test="is(i1=11)"]]the number is a multiple of 4[[elif test="is(i1=12)"]]the learner runs in the school 400 m race[[/if]].

generalfeedback.text:
Ask two questions. Can both happen at the same time? If not, the events are mutually exclusive. Does one happening change the probability of the other? If not, they are independent. Mutually exclusive events that can each happen are never independent: if one happens, the other cannot.

(a) [[if test="is(n1=1)"]]Mutually exclusive.[[elif test="is(n1=2)"]]Independent.[[else]]Neither.[[/if]] [[if test="is(i1=1)"]]If the die shows 2, it cannot show 5, so knowing one changes the probability of the other to 0. They are mutually exclusive, and so not independent.[[elif test="is(i1=2)"]]If Achieng goes by matatu, she cannot also go on foot, so knowing one changes the probability of the other to 0. They are mutually exclusive, and so not independent.[[elif test="is(i1=3)"]]If the number is odd, it cannot be a multiple of 10 (10 and 20 are even), so knowing one changes the probability of the other to 0. They are mutually exclusive, and so not independent.[[elif test="is(i1=4)"]]If the learner is in Grade 10, the learner cannot be in Grade 12, so knowing one changes the probability of the other to 0. They are mutually exclusive, and so not independent.[[elif test="is(i1=5)"]]The coin and the die do not affect each other: the die shows 6 with probability one in six whatever the coin shows. They are independent.[[elif test="is(i1=6)"]]The coin has no memory: the second toss is heads with probability one half whatever the first toss was. They are independent.[[elif test="is(i1=7)"]]The die in Kakamega cannot affect the spinner in Mombasa, so the events are independent.[[elif test="is(i1=8)"]]The seeds are in different counties, so whether one germinates does not change the chance for the other. They are independent.[[elif test="is(i1=9)"]]They are linked: the probability of an even score is one half, but of the scores less than 4 (1, 2 and 3) only one in three is even. So they are not independent.[[elif test="is(i1=10)"]]They are linked: rain makes a muddy road more likely, so they are not independent.[[elif test="is(i1=11)"]]They are linked: every multiple of 4 is even, so knowing the number is a multiple of 4 makes even certain. questiondescription.text:
Probability III: classifying pairs of events

Grade 12 CBE Essential 3.2: Decide whether two events are mutually exclusive, independent or neither, in everyday and dice contexts.

Essential

This question is based on the text of Chapter 3, Sections B and D of Cassell, D., Instone, S., Ling, J., Scruton, P. and Shilton, S., SMP AS/A2 Mathematics: Statistics 1 for Edexcel, Cambridge University Press, 2004: the definitions of mutually exclusive and independent events, applied to a bank of twelve new everyday event pairs.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Essential Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).
